Abstract.

We rigorously analyze the low temperature non-equilibrium dynamics of the East model, a special example of a one dimensional oriented kinetically constrained particle model, when the initial distribution is different from the reversible one and for times much smaller than the global relaxation time. This setting has been intensively studied in the physics literature to analyze the slow dynamics which follows a sudden quench from the liquid to the glass phase. In the limit of zero temperature (i.e. a vanishing density of vacancies) and for initial distributions such that the vacancies form a renewal process we prove that the density of vacancies, the persistence function and the two-time autocorrelation function behave as staircase functions with several plateaux. Furthermore the two-time autocorrelation function displays an aging behavior. We also provide a sharp description of the statistics of the domain length as a function of time, a domain being the interval between two consecutive vacancies. When the initial renewal process has finite mean our results confirm (and generalize) previous findings of the physicists for the restricted case of a product Bernoulli measure. However we show that a different behavior appears when the initial domain distribution is in the attraction domain of a α\alpha-stable law. All the above results actually follow from a more general result which says that the low temperature dynamics of the East model is very well described by that of a certain hierarchical coalescence process, a probabilistic object which can be viewed as a hierarchical sequence of suitably linked coalescence processes and whose asymptotic behavior has been recently studied in [14].

Mathematics Subject Classification: 60K35, 82C20.

Keywords: kinetically constrained models, non-equilibrium dynamics, coalescence, metastability, aging, interacting particle systems.

1. Introduction

Facilitated or kinetically constrained spin (particle) models (KCSM) are interacting particle systems which have been introduced in the physics literature [16, 17, 19] to model liquid/glass transition and more generally “glassy dynamics” (see e.g. [26, 20]). A configuration is given by assigning to each vertex xx of a (finite or infinite) connected graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} its occupation variable η⁡(x)∈{0,1}\eta(x)\in\{0,1\} which corresponds to an empty or filled site, respectively. The evolution is given by a Markovian stochastic dynamics of Glauber type. Each site with rate one refreshes its occupation variable to a filled or to an empty state with probability 1−q1-q or qq respectively provided that the current configuration around it satisfies an a priori specified constraint. For each site xx the corresponding constraint does not involve η⁡(x)\eta(x), thus detailed balance w.r.t. the Bernoulli(1−q1-q) product measure π\pi can be easily verified and the latter is an invariant reversible measure for the process.

One of the most studied KCSM is the East model [19]. It is a one-dimensional model (𝒢=ℤ\mathcal{G}={\mathbb{Z}} or 𝒢=ℤ+={0,1,…}\mathcal{G}={\mathbb{Z}}_{+}=\{0,1,\dots\}) and particle creation/annihilation at a given site xx can occur only if its right neighbor x+1x+1 is empty. The model is ergodic for any q≠0,1q\neq 0,1 with a positive spectral gap [1, 4] and it relaxes to the equilibrium reversible measure exponentially fast even when started from e.g. any non-trivial product measure [5]. However, as q↓0q\downarrow 0, the relaxation time Trelax​(q)T_{\rm relax}(q) diverges very fast, Trelax∼(exp⁡(λ​log⁡(1/q)2))T_{\rm relax}\sim\left(\exp(\lambda\log(1/q)^{2})\right) with a sharp constant λ\lambda (see [4]). A key issue, both from the mathematical and the physical point of view, is therefore that of describing accurately the evolution at q≪1q\ll 1 when the initial distribution is different from the reversible one and for time scales which are large but still much smaller than Trelax​(q)T_{\rm relax}(q) when the exponential relaxation to the reversible measure takes over.

An initial distribution which is often considered in the physics literature is the Bernoulli distribution at a density 1/21/2 [28, 27]. We refer the interested reader to [26, 21, 8, 18, 7] for the relevance of this setting in connection with the study of the liquidglass transition as well as for details for KCMS different from East model.

Let us give a rough picture of the non-equilibrium dynamics of the East model as q↓0q\downarrow 0. Since the equilibrium vacancy density is very small, most of the non-equilibrium evolution will try to remove the excess of vacancies present in the initial distribution and will thus be dominated by the coalescence of domains corresponding to the intervals separating two consecutive vacancies. Of course this process must necessarily occur in a kind of cooperative way because, in order to remove a vacancy, other vacancies must be created nearby (to its right). Since the creation of vacancies requires the overcoming of an energy barrier, in a first approximation the non-equilibrium dynamics of the East model for q≪1q\ll 1 is driven by a non-trivial energy landscape.

In order to better explain the structure of this landscape suppose that we start from a configuration with only two vacancies located at the sites aa and a+ℓa+\ell, with ℓ∈[2n−1+1,…,2n]\ell\in[2^{n-1}+1,\dots,2^{n}]. In this case a nice combinatorial argument (see [6] and also [27]) shows that, in order to remove the vacancy at aa within time tt, there must exists s≤ts\leq t such that the number of vacancies inside the interval (a,a+ℓ)(a,a+\ell) at time ss is at least nn. It is rather easy to show that at any given time ss the probability of observing nn vacancies in (a,a+ℓ)(a,a+\ell) is O⁡(qn)O(q^{n}) so that, in order to have a non negligible probability of observing the disappearance of the vacancy at aa, we need to wait an activation time tn=O⁡(1/qn)t_{n}=O(1/q^{n}). In a more physical language the energy barrier which the system must overcome is O⁡(log2⁡ℓ)O(\log_{2}\ell). As it is the case in many metastable phenomena, once the system decides to overcome the barrier and kill the vacancy, it does it in a time scale much smaller than the activation time. In our case this scale is tn−1=1/qn−1t_{n-1}=1/q^{n-1}.

The above argument indicates the following heuristic picture.

  1. (i)

    A hierarchical structure of the activation times tn=1/qnt_{n}=1/q^{n} (and of the energy landscape) well separated one from the other for q≪1q\ll 1.

  2. (ii)

    A kind of metastable behavior of the dynamics which removes vacancies in a hierarchical fashion.

  3. (iii)

    Since the characteristic time scales tnt_{n} are well separated one from the other, the evolution should show active and stalling periods. During the nt​hn^{th}-active period, identified with e.g. the interval [tn1−ϵ,tn1+ϵ][t_{n}^{1-\epsilon},t_{n}^{1+\epsilon}], ϵ≪1\epsilon\ll 1, only the vacancies with another vacancy to their right at distance less than 2n2^{n} can be removed. At the end of an active period no vacancies with distance less than 2n+12^{n}+1 are present anymore as well as no extra (i.e. not present at time t=0t=0) vacancies. During the nt​hn^{th}-stalling period [tn1+ϵ,tn+11−ϵ][t_{n}^{1+\epsilon},t_{n+1}^{1-\epsilon}] nothing interesting happens in the sense that none of the vacancies present at the beginning of the period are destroyed and no new vacancies are created at the end of the period.

Clear the above scenario, and particularly the presence of active and stalling periods, implies that physical quantities like the persistence function or the density of vacancies should behave as a staircase function with several plateaux and that aging should occur for two-time quantities as the two time-autocorrelation.

Such a general picture was somehow suggested in two interesting physics papers [28, 27] and some of the conclusions (properties (iv) above) were indeed observed in numerical simulations [28, 21]. In [28] the true East dynamics was replaced with that of a certain hierarchical coalescence model mimicking the features (i)–(iii) described above. In turn, under the assumption that the interval between two consecutive vacancies (domain) in the nn-th stalling period rescaled by 2n2^{n} has a well defined limiting distribution as n→∞n\to\infty, the form of this limiting distribution when the initial distribution is a Bernoulli product measure has been computed for the coalescence model.

Partly motivated by the above discussion and partly by other coalescence models in statistical physics with a mean field structure (see e.g. [10, 11, 12, 3]), the present authors introduced in [14] a large class of hierarchical coalescence models and: (1) proved the existence of a scaling limit under very general assumptions, (2) proved the universality of the scaling limit depending only on general features of the initial distribution and not on the details of the model. We refer the reader to Section 3 for more details and to [14] for a much more general setting.

In this paper, besides providing a mathematical derivation of the above mentioned heuristic picture, we rigorously establish aging and plateau behavior (Theorem 2.5). Furthermore (Theorem 2.6) we prove a scaling limit for: i) the inter-vacancy distance and ii) the position of the first vacancy for the model on the positive half line. In particular we prove that this scaling limit is universal if the initial renewal process has finite mean. If instead the initial distribution is the domain of attraction of an α\alpha-stable law, α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), the scaling limit is different and falls in another universality class depending on α\alpha. In order to establish the above results we actually prove a result which is more fundamental and of independent interest. Namely we show that with probability tending to one as q↓0q\downarrow 0, the non equilibrium dynamics of the East model starting from a renewal process is well approximated (in variation distance) by a suitable hierarchical coalescence process with rates depending on suitable large deviation probabilities of the East model (Theorem 3.8).

2. The East process: definition and main results

In what follows we will use the notation ℕ:=1,2,…{\mathbb{N}}:=1,2,\dots and ℤ+:=0,1,2,…{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}:=0,1,2,\dots. We will focus on the East process on ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} and explain in Section 7 how the result can be extended to the process defined on ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. The East process on ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} with parameter q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] is an interacting particle systems with a Glauber type dynamics on the configuration space Ω:={0,1}ℤ+\Omega:=\{0,1\}^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}, reversible with respect to the product probability measure π:=∏x∈ℤ+πx\pi:=\prod_{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}\pi_{x}, πx\pi_{x} being the Bernoulli(1−q)(1-q) measure. Since we are interested in the small qq regime throughout the following we will assume q≤1/2q\leq 1/2.

Remark 2.1.

Sometimes in the physical literature the parameter qq is written as q=e−β1+e−βq=\frac{e^{-\beta}}{1+e^{-\beta}} where β\beta is the inverse temperature so that the limit q↓0q\downarrow 0 corresponds to the zero temperature limit.

Elements of Ω\Omega will usually be denoted by the Greek letters σ,η,…\sigma,\eta,\dots and σ⁡(x)\sigma(x) will denote the occupancy variable at the site xx. The restriction of a configuration σ\sigma to a subset Λ\Lambda of ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} will be denoted by σΛ\sigma_{\Lambda}. The set of empty sites (or zeros in the sequel) of a configuration σ\sigma will be denoted by 𝒵⁡(σ)\mathcal{Z}(\sigma) and they will often be referred to as x0<x1<…x_{0}<x_{1}<\dots without the specification of the configuration if clear from the context.

The East process can be informally described as follows. Each vertex xx waits an independent mean one exponential time and then, provided that the current configuration σ\sigma satisfies the constraint σ⁡(x+1)=0\sigma(x+1)=0, the value of σ⁡(x)\sigma(x) is refreshed and set equal to 11 with probability 1−q1-q and to 00 with probability qq. Formally (see [22]) the process is uniquely specified by the action of its infinitesimal Markov generator ℒ\mathcal{L} on local (i.e. depending on finitely many variables) functions f:Ω↦ℝf:\Omega\mapsto{\mathbb{R}} that is given by

ℒ​f​(σ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}f(\sigma) =∑x∈ℤ+cx​(σ)​[πx​(f)−f⁡(σ)]\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}c_{x}(\sigma)\left[\pi_{x}(f)-f(\sigma)\right] (2.1)
=∑x∈ℤ+cx​(σ)​[(1−σ⁡(x))​(1−q)+σ⁡(x)​q]​(f⁡(σx)−f⁡(σ))\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}c_{x}(\sigma)\left[(1-\sigma(x))(1-q)+\sigma(x)q\right]\left(f(\sigma^{x})-f(\sigma)\right)

where cx​(σ):=1−σ⁡(x+1)c_{x}(\sigma):=1-\sigma(x+1) encodes the constraint, πx​(f)\pi_{x}(f) denotes the conditional mean π⁡(f|{σ⁡(y)}y≠x)\pi(f\thinspace|\thinspace\{\sigma(y)\}_{y\neq x}) and σx\sigma^{x} is obtained from σ\sigma by flipping its value at xx, i.e.

σx​(y)={σ⁡(y)if ​y≠x1−σ⁡(x)if ​y=x.\sigma^{x}(y)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\sigma(y)&\mbox{if }y\neq x\\ 1-\sigma(x)&\mbox{if }y=x\end{array}\right..

When the initial distribution at time t=0t=0 is QQ the law and expectation of the process on the Skohorod space D⁡([0,∞),Ω)D([0,\infty),\Omega) will be denoted by ℙQ{\mathbb{P}}_{Q} and 𝔼Q{\mathbb{E}}_{Q} respectively. If Q=δσQ=\delta_{\sigma} we write simply ℙσ{\mathbb{P}}_{\sigma}. In the sequel we will often write xk​(t)x_{k}(t) for the kt​hk^{th}-zero for the process σt\sigma_{t} at time tt if no confusion arises.

Definition 2.1.

Given two probability measures μ\mu on ℕ:=[1,2,…){\mathbb{N}}:=[1,2,\dots) and ν\nu on ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} we will write Q=Ren​(ν,μ)Q=\text{Ren}(\nu,\mu) if, under QQ, the first zero x0x_{0} has law ν\nu and it is independent of the random variables {xk−xk−1}k=1∞\{x_{k}-x_{k-1}\}_{k=1}^{\infty} which, in turn, form a sequence of i.i.d random variables with common law μ\mu. If ν=δ0\nu=\delta_{0} then we will write Q=Ren⁡(μ| 0)Q={\rm Ren}(\mu\thinspace|\thinspace 0).

Remark 2.2.

In most of the present paper the initial distribution QQ will always be assumed to be of the above form. For further generalizations we refer to Section 7.

The East process can also be defined on finite intervals Λ:=[a,b]⊂ℤ+\Lambda:=[a,b]\subset{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} provided that a suitable zero boundary condition is specified at the site b+1b+1. More precisely one defines the finite volume generator

ℒΛ​f​(σ)=∑x∈[a,b−1]cx​(σ)​[μx​(f)−f⁡(σ)]+[μb​(f)−f⁡(σ)]≡∑x∈ΛcxΛ​(σ)​[μx​(f)−f⁡(ω)],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\Lambda}f(\sigma)=\sum_{x\in[a,b-1]}c_{x}(\sigma)\left[\mu_{x}(f)-f(\sigma)\right]+\left[\mu_{b}(f)-f(\sigma)\right]\equiv\sum_{x\in\Lambda}c_{x}^{\Lambda}(\sigma)\left[\mu_{x}(f)-f(\omega)\right]\,,
wherecxΛ​(σ)={1−σ⁡(x+1)for x∈[a,b−1]1if x=b\displaystyle\text{where}\quad c_{x}^{\Lambda}(\sigma)=\begin{cases}1-\sigma(x+1)&\text{for $x\in[a,b-1]$}\\ 1&\text{if $x=b$}\end{cases} (2.2)

In particular there is no constraint at site bb, a fact that pictorially we can interpret by saying that there is a frozen zero at site b+1b+1. This frozen zero is the above mentioned boundary condition. In this case the process is nothing but a continuous time Markov chain reversible w.r.t. the product measure πΛ:=∏x∈[a,b]πx\pi_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{x\in[a,b]}\pi_{x} and, due to the “East” character of the constraint, for any initial condition η\eta its evolution coincides with that of the East process in ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} (restricted to Λ\Lambda) starting from the configuration

We will use the self-explanatory notation ℙQΛ{\mathbb{P}}_{Q}^{\Lambda} (or ℙσΛ{\mathbb{P}}_{\sigma}^{\Lambda}) for the law of the process starting from the law QQ (from σ\sigma).

2.0.1. Additional notation

In the sequel Λ\Lambda will always denote a finite interval of ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} with endpoints 0≤a<b<∞0\leq a<b<\infty.

It will also be quite useful to isolate some special configurations in ΩΛ\Omega_{\Lambda}. We denote by σ0​𝟙\sigma_{0\mathds{1}} the configuration in ΩΛ:={0,1}Λ\Omega_{\Lambda}:=\{0,1\}^{\Lambda} such that 𝒵⁡(σ)={a}\mathcal{Z}(\sigma)=\{a\} and by σ𝟙\sigma_{\mathds{1}} the configuration with 𝒵⁡(σ)=∅\mathcal{Z}(\sigma)=\emptyset. In words, σ0​𝟙\sigma_{0\mathds{1}} is the configuration with a single zero located at the left extreme of the interval, while σ𝟙\sigma_{\mathds{1}} is the configuration with no zeros. We also let, with a slight abuse of notation, ℙ0​𝟙Λ:=ℙσ0​𝟙Λ{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}:={\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}} and ℙ𝟙Λ:=ℙσ𝟙Λ{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\mathds{1}}:={\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma_{\mathds{1}}}.

2.1. Graphical construction

Here we recall a standard graphical construction which allows to define on the same probability space the finite volume East process for all initial conditions. Using a standard percolation argument [13, 23] together with the fact that the constraints cxc_{x} are uniformly bounded and of finite range, it is not difficult to see that the graphical construction can be extended without problems also to the infinite volume case. Given a finite interval Λ⊂ℤ+\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} we associate to each x∈Λx\in\Lambda a Poisson process of parameter one and, independently, a family of independent Bernoulli(1−q)(1-q) random variables {sx,k:k∈ℕ}\{s_{x,k}:k\in{\mathbb{N}}\}. The occurrences of the Poisson process associated to xx will be denoted by {tx,k:k∈ℕ}\{t_{x,k}:\ k\in{\mathbb{N}}\}. We assume independence as xx varies in Λ\Lambda. Notice that with probability one all the occurrences {tx,k}k∈ℕ,x∈ℤ+\{t_{x,k}\}_{k\in{\mathbb{N}},\,x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}} are different. This defines the probability space. The corresponding probability measure will be denoted by ℙ{\mathbb{P}}. Given an initial configuration η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega we construct a Markov process (σtΛ,η)t≥0(\sigma_{t}^{\Lambda,\eta})_{t\geq 0} on the above probability space satisfying σt=0Λ,η=η\sigma^{\Lambda,\eta}_{t=0}=\eta according to the following rules. At each time t=tx,nt=t_{x,n} the site xx queries the state of its own constraint cxΛc^{\Lambda}_{x}. If the constraint is satisfied, i.e. if σt−Λ,η​(x+1)=0\sigma^{\Lambda,\eta}_{t-}(x+1)=0, then tx,nt_{x,n} will be called a legal ring and at time tt the configuration resets its value at site xx to the value of the corresponding Bernoulli variable sx,ns_{x,n}. We stress here that the rings and coin tosses at xx for s≤ts\leq t have no influence whatsoever on the evolution of the configuration at the sites which enter in its constraint (here x+1x+1) and thus they have no influence of whether a ring at xx for s>ts>t is legal or not. It is easy to check that the above construction actually gives a continuous time Markov chain with generator (2.2).

A first immediate consequence is the following decoupling property.

Lemma 2.2.

Fix c<a<b<dc<a<b<d with a,b,c,d∈ℤ+∪{∞}a,b,c,d\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}\cup\{\infty\} and let Λ=[c,d],Λ′=[a,b],V=[b+1,d]\Lambda=[c,d],\ \Lambda^{\prime}=[a,b],\ V=[b+1,d]. Take two events 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and ℬ{\mathcal{B}}, belonging respectively to the σ\sigma–algebra generated by {σs​(x)}s​⩽​t,x∈Λ′\{\sigma_{s}(x)\}_{s\;\leqslant\;t,\,x\in\Lambda^{\prime}} and {σs​(x)}s​⩽​t,x∈V\{\sigma_{s}(x)\}_{s\;\leqslant\;t,\,x\in V}. Then, for any σ∈ΩΛ\sigma\in\Omega_{\Lambda}, (i) ℙσΛ​(ℬ)=ℙσVV​(ℬ){\mathbb{P}}_{\sigma}^{\Lambda}({\mathcal{B}})={\mathbb{P}}_{\sigma_{V}}^{V}({\mathcal{B}}); (ii) ℙσΛ(𝒜∩ℬ∩{σsΛ(b+1)=0∀s⩽t})=ℙσΛ′Λ′(𝒜)ℙσVV(ℬ∩{σsV(b+1)=0∀s⩽t}).{\mathbb{P}}_{\sigma}^{\Lambda}({\mathcal{A}}\cap{\mathcal{B}}\cap\{\sigma_{s}^{\Lambda}(b+1)=0~\forall s\;\leqslant\;t\})={\mathbb{P}}_{\sigma_{\Lambda^{\prime}}}^{\Lambda^{\prime}}({\mathcal{A}}){\mathbb{P}}_{\sigma_{V}}^{V}({\mathcal{B}}\cap\{\sigma_{s}^{V}(b+1)=0~\forall s\;\leqslant\;t\})\,.

The last, simple but quite important consequence of the graphical construction is the following one. Assume that the zeros of the starting configuration σ\sigma are labeled in increasing order as x0,x1,…,xnx_{0},x_{1},\dots,x_{n} and define τ\tau as the first time at which one the xix_{i}’s is killed, i.e. the occupation variable there flips to one. Then, up to time τ\tau the East dynamics factorizes over the East process in each interval [xi,xi+1)[x_{i},x_{i+1}).

2.2. Ergodicity

The finite volume East process is trivially ergodic because of the frozen zero boundary condition (see 2.2). The infinite volume process in ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} is ergodic in the sense that 00 is a simple eigenvalue of the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} thought of as a selfadjoint operator on L2​(Ω,π)L^{2}(\Omega,\pi) [4]. As far as more quantitative results are concerned we recall the following (see [4] for part (i) and [5] for part (ii)).

Theorem 2.3.
  1. (i)

    The generator (2.1) has a positive spectral gap, denoted by gap(ℒ)\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}), such that

    limq↓0log⁡(gap(ℒ)−1)/(log⁡(1/q))2=(2​log​2)−1.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}\log(\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L})^{-1})/\left(\log(1/q)\right)^{2}=(2\log 2)^{-1}.

    Moreover, for any interval Λ\Lambda, the spectral gap of the finite volume generator ℒΛ\mathcal{L}_{\Lambda} is not smaller than gap(ℒ)\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}).

  2. (ii)

    Assume that the initial distribution QQ is a product Bernoulli(α\alpha) measure, α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). Then there exists m∈(0,gap(ℒ)]m\in(0,\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L})] and for any local function ff there exists a constant CfC_{f} such that

    |𝔼Q​(f⁡(σt))−π⁡(f)|≤Cf​e−m​t|{\mathbb{E}}_{Q}(f(\sigma_{t}))-\pi(f)|\leq C_{f}e^{-mt}

The above results show that relaxation to equilibrium is indeed taking place at an exponential rate on a time scale Trelax=gap(ℒ)−1T_{\rm relax}=\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L})^{-1} which however, for small values of qq, is very large and of the order of ec​log⁡(1/q)2e^{c\log(1/q)^{2}} with c=(2​log⁡2)−1c=(2\log 2)^{-1}.

2.3. Main results: plateau behavior, aging and scaling limits

We are now ready to state our first set of results (Theorem 2.5 and 2.6) which details the non equilibrium behavior of the East process for small values of qq (small temperature) and for time scales much smaller that TrelaxT_{\rm relax}. The prove of both theorems is detailed in Section 6 and is obtained thanks to the approximation of the East model with a suitable coalescence process. The definition of this coalescence process and the approximation result (Theorem 3.8), which is indeed the heart of our paper, is instead stated in Section 3 and proven in Section 5.

Definition 2.4.

Given ϵ,q∈(0,1)\epsilon,\,q\in(0,1), we set

t0:=1;t0−:=0;t0+=(1q)ϵ\displaystyle t_{0}:=1;~~~~~t_{0}^{-}:=0;~~~~~t_{0}^{+}=\left(\frac{1}{q}\right)^{\epsilon}
tn:=(1q)n;tn−:=tn1−ε;tn+=tn1+ε∀n⩾ 1.\displaystyle t_{n}:=\left(\frac{1}{q}\right)^{n};~~~~~t_{n}^{-}:=t_{n}^{1-\varepsilon};~~~~~t_{n}^{+}=t_{n}^{1+\varepsilon}\,\,\,\,\,\,\forall n\;\geqslant\;1\,. (2.4)

The time interval [tn−,tn+][t_{n}^{-},t_{n}^{+}] and [tn+,tn+1−][t_{n}^{+},t_{n+1}^{-}] will be called respectively the nt​hn^{th}-active period and the nt​hn^{th}-stalling period.

Theorem 2.5 (Persistence, vacancy density and two-time autocorrelations during stalling periods: plateau and aging).

The above result holds also for Q=Ren⁡(ν,μ)Q={\rm Ren}(\nu,\mu), which can be obtained from Q=Ren⁡(μ| 0)Q={\rm Ren}(\mu\thinspace|\thinspace 0) by a random shifting of law ν\nu. 3. Hierarchical Coalescence and the East process

In this section we introduce a hierarchical coalescence process (in the sequel HCP) which belongs to a much larger class of processes whose definition, asymptotic behavior and scaling limits are stated and analyzed in [14]. We will then state a result (Theorem 3.8) which had been conjectured in [28] which says that in the low temperature limit q↓0q\downarrow 0 the East process is well described by HCP. This result, together with the knowledge of the asymptotic behavior for HCP detailed in Section 3.4, will be the key to prove our main results for the East model announced in the previous section (Theorem 2.5 and 2.6).

Before giving a formal definition of HCP we start by saying that of the main features of HCP is that time has a hierarchical nature. There is an infinite sequence of epochs and inside each epoch the time runs from 00 to ∞\infty. The HCP inside one epoch is just a suitable coalescence process dependent on the label of the epoch. The overall evolution is obtained by suitably linking consecutive epochs in the obvious way: the end (i.e. the limit t→∞t\to\infty) of one epoch coincides with the beginning of the next one. The key link between the HCP we propose below and the East process is provided by the very specific choice of the coalescence rates for the nt​hn^{th}-epoch process. As it will be apparent below these rates are expressed in terms of suitable large deviation probabilities of the East process.

3.1. Domains and classes

In order to define our HCP we need to fix some notation and introduce some basic geometric concepts.

Definition 3.1.

Given a configuration σ∈Ω\sigma\in\Omega we say that the interval [c,d]⊂ℤ+[c,d]\subset{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}, c<dc<d, is a domain of σ\sigma if σ⁡(x)=1\sigma(x)=1 for any xx, c<x<dc<x<d, and σ⁡(c)=σ⁡(d)=0\sigma(c)=\sigma(d)=0. If σ∈ΩΛ\sigma\in\Omega_{\Lambda} for some finite or infinite interval Λ⊂ℤ+\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} then the domains of σ\sigma are defined as the domains of the extended configuration σ~∈Ω\tilde{\sigma}\in\Omega, given in (2.3), which are contained in [a,b+1][a,b+1]. In particular, if −∞<a​⩽​b<∞-\infty<a\;\leqslant\;b<\infty, the domains of σ\sigma are the finite intervals [c,d][c,d] where σ\sigma appears as 0,1,…,1,00,1,\dots,1,0 as well as the interval [u,b+1][u,b+1], where uu is the rightmost zero of σ\sigma. Given a domain [c,d][c,d] its length is defined as d−cd-c, while given a zero (empty site) xx of σ\sigma the length of the domain having xx as left extreme is denoted by dxd_{x}.

Next we partition ℕ{\mathbb{N}} by the sets 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} defined by

𝒞0={1}𝒞n=[2n−1+1,2n]​ for ​n​⩾​ 1.\mathcal{C}_{0}=\{1\}\,\qquad\mathcal{C}_{n}=[2^{n-1}+1,2^{n}]\;\text{ for }n\;\geqslant\;1\,. (3.1)

and we set

𝒞⩾​n:=(∪m​⩾​n𝒞m),𝒞>n:=(∪m>n𝒞m),𝒞⩽​n:=∪m=0n𝒞n.\mathcal{C}_{\;\geqslant\;n}:=\bigl(\cup_{m\;\geqslant\;n}\mathcal{C}_{m}\bigr)\,,\qquad\mathcal{C}_{>n}:=\bigl(\cup_{m>n}\mathcal{C}_{m}\bigr)\,,\qquad\mathcal{C}_{\;\leqslant\;n}:=\cup_{m=0}^{n}\mathcal{C}_{n}\,.
Definition 3.2.

Given a configuration σ\sigma in Ω\Omega or ΩΛ\Omega_{\Lambda}, we say that a domain of σ\sigma is of class nn (respectively, at least nn, larger than nn, at most nn) if its length belongs to 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} (respectively, 𝒞⩾​n\mathcal{C}_{\;\geqslant\;n}, 𝒞>n\mathcal{C}_{>n}, 𝒞⩽​n\mathcal{C}_{\;\leqslant\;n}). We also say that a zero (empty site) xx of σ\sigma is of class nn if dx∈𝒞nd_{x}\in\mathcal{C}_{n}. Similar definitions hold for 𝒞⩾​n,𝒞>n,𝒞⩽​n\mathcal{C}_{\;\geqslant\;n},\mathcal{C}_{>n},\mathcal{C}_{\;\leqslant\;n}.

Finally, we point out a simple property of the sets 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n}, which will be crucial in our investigation:

d,d′∈𝒞n⇒d+d′∈𝒞>n,∀n​⩾​ 0.d,d^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{n}\;\Rightarrow\;d+d^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{>n}\,,\qquad\forall n\;\geqslant\;0\,. (3.2)

In what follows we introduce (hierarchical) coalescence processes as jump stochastic dynamics on Ω\Omega, where jumps correspond to filling an empty site. The term coalescence is justified. Indeed, a configuration σ∈Ω\sigma\in\Omega is univocally determined by the set 𝒵⁡(σ)\mathcal{Z}(\sigma) of its zeros. Filling the empty site xx in a configuration σ\sigma corresponds to removing the point xx from the set 𝒵⁡(σ)\mathcal{Z}(\sigma). Since a domain is simply the interval between consecutive zeros in 𝒵⁡(σ)\mathcal{Z}(\sigma), removing the point x∈𝒵⁡(σ)x\in\mathcal{Z}(\sigma) corresponds to the coalescence of the domains on the left and on the right of xx.

3.2. The nt​hn^{th}-epoch coalescence process

We describe here the one–epoch coalescence process associated to the nt​hn^{th}-epoch (shortly nt​hn^{th}-CP), which depends also on the parameters q,ε∈(0,1)q,\varepsilon\in(0,1). Fixed these parameters, we define

T0:=q(1−ϵ)/2,T1:=1/q3​ϵ,Tn:=(1/q)(n−1)​(1+3​ε)​for​n​⩾​ 2.T_{0}:=q^{(1-\epsilon)/2}\,,\qquad T_{1}:=1/q^{3\epsilon}\,,\qquad T_{n}:=(1/q)^{(n-1)(1+3\varepsilon)}~~{\mbox{for}}~~n\;\geqslant\;2\,. (3.3)

Then for each n​⩾​ 0n\;\geqslant\;0 we define the function λn:ℕ→[0,∞)\lambda_{n}:{\mathbb{N}}\to[0,\infty) as

λn​(d):={−Tn−1​log⁡(ℙ0​𝟙[0,d−1]​(σs​(0)=0​∀s∈[0,Tn]))if ​d∈𝒞n,0otherwise.\lambda_{n}(d):=\begin{cases}-T_{n}^{-1}\log\left({\mathbb{P}}_{0\mathds{1}}^{[0,d-1]}\left(\sigma_{s}(0)=0\,\forall s\in[0,T_{n}]\right)\right)&\mbox{if }d\in\mathcal{C}_{n}\,,\\ 0&\mbox{otherwise}\,.\end{cases} (3.4)

where, we emphasize, ℙ0​𝟙[0,d−1]​(⋅){\mathbb{P}}_{0\mathds{1}}^{[0,d-1]}\left(\cdot\right) refers to the East process in Λ=[0,d−1]\Lambda=[0,d-1], starting from the configuration σ0​𝟙\sigma_{0\mathds{1}} and evolving with parameter qq.

Finally we write Ω(≥n)\Omega^{(\geq n)} for the set of configurations in Ω\Omega whose domains are all of class at least nn. Then the nt​hn^{th}-CP is a Markov process with paths in the Skohorod space D⁡([0,∞),Ω(≥n))D([0,\infty),\Omega^{(\geq n)}) whose infinitesimal generator ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n} acts on local functions as

ℒnf(σ)=∑x∈ℤ+:σ⁡(x)=0λn(dx)(f(σx)−f(σ)).\mathcal{L}_{n}f(\sigma)=\sum_{x\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}:\sigma(x)=0}\lambda_{n}(d_{x})\bigl(f(\sigma^{x})-f(\sigma)\bigr)\,. (3.5)

Above, σx\sigma^{x} is the configuration obtained from σ\sigma by flipping its value in xx, i.e. by filling the empty site xx (we refer to the case σ⁡(x)=0\sigma(x)=0). We will write ℙσC,n{\mathbb{P}}^{C,n}_{\sigma} for the law of the nt​hn^{th}-CP starting from the configuration σ\sigma.

As observed in [14], for almost all random paths {σs}s​⩾​ 0\{\sigma_{s}\}_{s\;\geqslant\;0} of the nt​hn^{th}-CP, the asymptotic configuration σ∞\sigma_{\infty} defined as σ∞​(x)=lims↑∞σs​(x)\sigma_{\infty}(x)=\lim_{s\uparrow\infty}\sigma_{s}(x) exists and it belongs to Ω(≥n+1)⊂Ω(≥n)\Omega^{(\geq n+1)}\subset\Omega^{(\geq n)}. Hence, in what follows, trajectories of the nt​hn^{th}-CP will be thought of up to time t=∞t=\infty included.

3.3. The hierarchical coalescence process (HCP)

Fix the parameters q,ε∈(0,1)q,\varepsilon\in(0,1).

Definition 3.3.

The HCP starting from the configuration σ∈Ω\sigma\in\Omega is the stochastic process whose evolution is described by a sequence of random paths

(σs(n):s∈[0,∞])n∈ℤ+∈D([0,+∞],Ω)ℤ+,(\sigma^{(n)}_{s}\,:\,s\in[0,\infty])_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}\in D([0,+\infty],\Omega)^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}\,,

such that (inductively over nn) {σs(n)}s≥0\{\sigma^{(n)}_{s}\}_{s\geq 0} is a random path of the nt​hn^{th}-CP starting from σ\sigma if n=0n=0 and from σ∞(n−1)\sigma^{(n-1)}_{\infty} if n​⩾​ 1n\;\geqslant\;1.

If the initial configuration (i.e. at time t=0t=0 in the first epoch) has law QQ then the corresponding law and expectation for the HCP will be denoted by ℙQH{\mathbb{P}}^{H}_{Q} and 𝔼QH{\mathbb{E}}^{H}_{Q} respectively. In Section 3.3.1 below we present a refined graphical construction, allowing to define on the same probability space all the HCP as the initial configuration varies in Ω\Omega.

Remark 3.1.

We point out that the HCP defined here corresponds to the one in [14] with the choice λℓ(n):=0\lambda^{(n)}_{\ell}:=0, λr(n):=λn−1\lambda^{(n)}_{r}:=\lambda_{n-1} and d(n)=2n−2+1d^{(n)}=2^{n-2}+1 for n​⩾​ 2n\;\geqslant\;2, d(1)=1d^{(1)}=1. Note that the index of epochs in the formulation of [14] runs over ℕ{\mathbb{N}} while here it runs over ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} (the HCP process (ξs(n):s∈[0,∞])n∈ℕ∈D([0,+∞],Ω)ℕ(\xi^{(n)}_{s}\,:\,s\in[0,\infty])_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}\in D([0,+\infty],\Omega)^{{\mathbb{N}}}\, defined in [14] and with the former choices of the rates is such that, for any n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and s∈[0,∞]s\in[0,\infty], ξn\xi^{n} has the same law of σsn−1\sigma^{n-1}_{s}).

One can define the HCP in the finite volume Λ=[a,b]\Lambda=[a,b] as the process whose evolution is described by a sequence of random paths

(σs(n):s∈[0,∞])n∈ℤ+∈D(ℝ¯+,ΩΛ)ℤ+(\sigma^{(n)}_{s}\,:\,s\in[0,\infty])_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}\in D(\bar{\mathbb{R}}_{+},\Omega_{\Lambda})^{{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}}

obtained by observing in the interval Λ\Lambda the infinite volume HCP starting at the configuration σ~\tilde{\sigma} defined in (2.3). The corresponding law with initial distribution QQ will be denoted by ℙQΛ,H{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda,H}_{Q}.

3.3.1. Graphical construction

As for the East process we describe a graphical construction of the HCP in finite volume. A similar construction holds also in the infinite volume case again using the results in [13, 23].

Given an interval Λ⊂ℤ+\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} we associate to each x∈Λx\in\Lambda and to each n∈ℤ+n\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} a Poisson process of parameter one and, independently, a family {Sx,k(n):k∈ℕ}\{S^{(n)}_{x,k}:k\in{\mathbb{N}}\} of independent random variables uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1]. We assume independence as xx and nn vary. The occurrences of the Poisson process associated to the pair (x,n)(x,n) will be denoted by (tx,k(n):k​⩾​ 0)(t^{(n)}_{x,k}:k\;\geqslant\;0). The above construction defines the probability space whose probability measure is denoted by ℙ{\mathbb{P}}. The construction of the path (σtn:t∈[0,∞])n​⩾​ 0(\sigma^{n}_{t}:t\in[0,\infty])_{n\;\geqslant\;0} of the HCP with initial condition σ\sigma then proceeds by induction on nn. Set σ0(0)=σ\sigma^{(0)}_{0}=\sigma. At each time t=tx,k(0)t=t^{(0)}_{x,k}, k=1,2,…k=1,2,\dots, if σt−(0)​(x)=0\sigma^{(0)}_{t-}(x)=0 and if Sx,k(0)​⩽​λ0​(dx​(σt−(0)))S^{(0)}_{x,k}\;\leqslant\;\lambda_{0}(d_{x}(\sigma^{(0)}_{t-})) then the configuration σt(0)\sigma^{(0)}_{t} is obtained from σt−(0)\sigma^{(0)}_{t-} by filling the site xx. In this case, the occurrence tx,k(0)t^{(0)}_{x,k} is called legal ring. Otherwise σt(0):=σt−(0)\sigma^{(0)}_{t}:=\sigma^{(0)}_{t-}. Clearly the limiting configuration σ∞(0)\sigma^{(0)}_{\infty} is well defined a.s.. The path (σt(1))t∈[0,∞](\sigma^{(1)}_{t})_{t\in[0,\infty]} is then defined exactly in the same way by replacing the initial configuration σ\sigma with σ∞(0)\sigma^{(0)}_{\infty}. The construction is then repeated inductively.

3.3.2. Characteristic time scales

Before moving on with the main results for the HCP we pause for a moment and establish some quantitative bounds on the characteristic time scales of the process. Although such results are completely irrelevant for the asymptotic as n→∞n\to\infty of the HCP they will play a crucial role when we will compare the HCP with the East process.

Lemma 3.4.

Fix N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}. Consider the nt​hn^{th}-CP with parameters qq and ε:=1/8​N\varepsilon:=1/8N in the definition (3.3). Then there exists a finite constant c=c⁡(N,L)c=c(N,L) such that, for any n≤Nn\leq N,

ctn​⩽​mind∈𝒞n​λn​(d)​⩽​maxd∈𝒞n​λn​(d)≤1c​tn.\frac{c}{t_{n}}\;\leqslant\;\min_{d\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}\lambda_{n}(d)\;\leqslant\;\max_{d\in\mathcal{C}_{n}}\lambda_{n}(d)\leq\frac{1}{c\,t_{n}}\,. (3.6)
Proof.

The proof is based on the results of Section 4 and it can be skipped on a first reading.

Let τ~\tilde{\tau} be the hitting time of the set {σ(0)=1}\{\sigma(0)=1\} for the East process with parameter qq and let Λ=[0,d−1]\Lambda=[0,d-1] with d∈𝒞nd\in\mathcal{C}_{n}. Fix n≤Nn\leq N , then using (4.7) we get

ℙ01Λ​(τ~≥Tn)=1−ℙ01Λ​(τ~​⩽​Tn)​⩾​ 1−c​Tn/tn{\mathbb{P}}_{01}^{\Lambda}(\tilde{\tau}\geq T_{n})=1-{\mathbb{P}}_{01}^{\Lambda}(\tilde{\tau}\;\leqslant\;T_{n})\;\geqslant\;1-c\,T_{n}/t_{n} (3.7)

and the second half of (3.6) follows. In order to prove the lower bound we write

ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(σs​(0)=0​∀s∈[0,Tn])=ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ~​⩾​Tn)\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}_{0\mathds{1}}^{\Lambda}(\sigma_{s}(0)=0\,\forall s\in[0,T_{n}])={\mathbb{P}}_{0\mathds{1}}^{\Lambda}(\tilde{\tau}\;\geqslant\;T_{n})
=ℙ0​𝟙Λ({τ~⩾Tn}∩{σTn=σ0​𝟙})+ℙ0​𝟙Λ({τ~⩾Tn}∩{σTn≠σ0​𝟙}).\displaystyle={\mathbb{P}}_{0\mathds{1}}^{\Lambda}(\{\tilde{\tau}\;\geqslant\;T_{n}\}\cap\{\sigma_{T_{n}}=\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}\})+{\mathbb{P}}_{0\mathds{1}}^{\Lambda}(\{\tilde{\tau}\;\geqslant\;T_{n}\}\cap\{\sigma_{T_{n}}\neq\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}\})\,. (3.8)

For i=1,2i=1,2 let FiF_{i} be a random variable with values in some set EE (the same for i=1,2i=1,2) on some probability space (Θi,ℱi,ℙi)(\Theta_{i},\mathcal{F}_{i},{\mathbb{P}}_{i}). Then we define

dT​V​({F1,ℙ1},{F2,ℙ2}):=dT​V​(𝔭1,𝔭2),d_{TV}(\{F_{1},{\mathbb{P}}_{1}\};\{F_{2},{\mathbb{P}}_{2}\}):=d_{TV}(\mathfrak{p}_{1},\mathfrak{p}_{2})\,,

where 𝔭i\mathfrak{p}_{i} denotes the law of FiF_{i} and dT​V​(⋅,⋅)d_{TV}(\cdot,\cdot) denotes the total variation distance.

limq↓0supt∈[0,tN+]dT​V​({σt,ℙQΛ},{σtH,ℙQΛ,H})=0.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}\,\sup_{t\in[0,t_{N}^{+}]}\,d_{TV}\bigl(\{\sigma_{t},\,{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{Q}\};\,\{\sigma^{H}_{t},\,{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda,H}_{Q}\}\bigr)=0\,.\hfill\penalty (3.24)

Let Q=Ren​(ν,μ)Q=\text{Ren}(\nu,\mu) with μ\mu such that, for any n≥1n\geq 1, μ⁡([n,∞))>0\mu\left([n,\infty)\right)>0. In the same assumption of Theorem 3.7 and for any k≥0k\geq 0

Assume that the (m+δ)t​h(m+\delta)^{th}-moment of μ\mu and ν\nu is finite for some δ>0\delta>0. Then

Remark 3.3.

The above theorem is really a corollary of Theorem 3.7 once we prove a strong finite volume approximation result both for the East process and for the HCP on ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}. More precisely we will show that, up to time tN+t_{N}^{+}, the law (and the moments) of the first kk zeros, in the limit q↓0q\downarrow 0, is very well approximated by the corresponding law (and moments) of the finite volume processes provided that the chosen volume is large enough (see Propositions 4.12, 4.13 in Section 4.2). The assumption μ⁡([k,∞))>0\mu\left([k,\infty)\right)>0 for any integer kk is there exactly in order to greatly simplify the proof of such an approximation. Without it the result still holds but its proof requires more lengthy arguments which will appear elsewhere [15].

4. Preliminary results for the low temperature East process

In this section we establish some results for the low temperature East process which will be crucial to prove the approximation with HCP in the following section. Unless otherwise specified, we set Λ:=[0,L−1]\Lambda:=[0,L-1] with L​⩾​ 1L\;\geqslant\;1\, which is fixed once and for all and does not change as q↓0q\downarrow 0. Let us begin by reviewing some known properties (Lemma 4.1 and Remark 4.1) which will have a fundamental role in what follows.

Recall that a site xj∈𝒵⁡(σ)x_{j}\in\mathcal{Z}(\sigma) is said to be of class nn if xj+1−xj∈𝒞n=[2n−1+1,2n]x_{j+1}-x_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{n}=[2^{n-1}+1,2^{n}]. The next combinatorial lemma (see also [28, 27]) says that the minimal number of extra zeros that we have to create in order to kill a zero of class nn is nn.

Lemma 4.1.

[6] Consider the East process on Λ:=[0,L−1]\Lambda:=[0,L-1] starting from the completely filled configuration σ𝟙\sigma_{\mathds{1}}. For n​⩾​ 1n\;\geqslant\;1 let V⁡(n)V(n) be the set of configurations that the process can reach under the condition that, at any given time, no more than nn zeros are present. Define

ℓ⁡(n):=supσ∈V⁡(n)(L−x0)\ell(n):=\sup_{\sigma\in V(n)}(L-x_{0})

where x0=x0​(σ)x_{0}=x_{0}(\sigma) is the smallest element of 𝒵⁡(σ)\mathcal{Z}(\sigma). Then ℓ⁡(n)=2n−1\ell(n)=2^{n}-1 for all L≥2n−1L\geq 2^{n}-1.

Remark 4.1.

If instead of considering a frozen zero boundary condition at LL we consider a deterministic time-dependent boundary condition σt​(L)∈{0,1}\sigma_{t}(L)\in\{0,1\}, the above lemma implies that ℓ⁡(n)≤2n−1\ell(n)\leq 2^{n}-1 for L≥2n+1L\geq 2^{n}+1. A key consequence is the following. Let xj∈𝒵⁡(σ)x_{j}\in\mathcal{Z}(\sigma) be of class n​⩾​ 1n\;\geqslant\;1. By definition dj=xj+1−xjd_{j}=x_{j+1}-x_{j} belongs to the interval [2n−1+1,2n][2^{n-1}+1,2^{n}]. Define TjT_{j} to be the first time the site xjx_{j} is filled, then at TjT_{j} there must be a zero at xj+1x_{j}+1. Thus there must exists an intermediate time t∈[0,Tj]t\in[0,T_{j}] such that, at time tt there are at least nn zeros in the interval [xj+1,xj+1−1][x_{j}+1,x_{j+1}-1]. Not surprisingly that will force the characteristic time scale of TjT_{j} to be of the order of 1/qn1/q^{n}.

4.1. Energy barriers and characteristic time scales

We start by establishing two results which say that, in the limit q↓0q\downarrow 0 and at any given time, the probability of observing kk zeros which were not present at t=0t=0 is O⁡(qk)O(q^{k}) (see Lemma 4.2). Therefore the probability of the event {σt(x)=0}\{\sigma_{t}(x)=0\} coincides, for q≈0q\approx 0, with the probability of the event that a zero has persisted at xx for the whole interval [0,t][0,t] (Lemma 4.3).

Then we analyze the East process starting from the special configuration σ0​𝟙\sigma_{0\mathds{1}} having a single zero located at the origin. We study two important stopping times. The first, τ~\tilde{\tau}, is the first time that the origin is filled (i.e. the zero at the origin is removed) while the second, τ𝟙\tau_{\mathds{1}}, is the hitting time of the completely filled configuration σ𝟙\sigma_{\mathds{1}}. We obtain upper and lower bounds on the characteristic time scales of these random times (see Lemma 4.4), which are optimal in the limit q↓0q\downarrow 0 (Remark 4.2). As a consequence we establish upper bounds on the probability of observing at time tt a zero of class nn (Corollary 4.5) and of killing at least one or at least two zeros of class nn in a time interval tt (Corollary 4.6 and 4.7, respectively). Finally we prove that τ~\tilde{\tau}, after a proper rescaling, weakly converges in the limit q↓0q\downarrow 0 to an exponential variable of parameter 11 (Lemma 4.11 and Remark 4.4).

Lemma 4.2.

Fix σ∈ΩΛ\sigma\in\Omega_{\Lambda}\,, t​⩾​ 0t\;\geqslant\;0 and k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}. Let V=[0,a]⊂ΛV=[0,a]\subset\Lambda and let {y1,…,yk}⊂V∖𝒵⁡(σ)\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}\subset V\setminus\mathcal{Z}(\sigma). Let finally ℱ\mathcal{F} be the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the Poisson processes and coin tosses in Λ∖V\Lambda\setminus V. Then

ℙσΛ​({y1,…,yk}⊂𝒵⁡(σt)|ℱ)​⩽​qk.{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\bigl(\bigl\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})\thinspace|\thinspace\mathcal{F}\bigr)\;\leqslant\;q^{k}\,. (4.1)

Moreover

ℙσΛ(∃s≤t:{y1,…,yk}⊂𝒵(σt)|ℱ)⩽atqk.{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\bigl(\exists\,s\leq t:\ \bigl\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})\thinspace|\thinspace\mathcal{F}\bigr)\;\leqslant\;atq^{k}\,. (4.2)

The same results hold when Λ\Lambda is replaced by ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}.

Proof.

We appeal to the graphical construction of Section 2.1. Let y1,…,yky_{1},\dots,y_{k} be as in the lemma, labeled in increasing order. Given m​⩾​ 0m\;\geqslant\;0, we write 𝒜m\mathcal{A}_{m} for the event that the last legal ring at y1y_{1} before time tt, which is well defined because y1∈𝒵⁡(σt)∖𝒵⁡(σ)y_{1}\in\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})\setminus\mathcal{Z}(\sigma), occurs at time ty1,mt_{y_{1},m}. Recall that (i) at the time ty1,mt_{y_{1},m} the current configuration resets its value at y1y_{1} to the value of an independent Bernoulli(1−q)(1-q) random variable sy1,ms_{y_{1},m} and (ii) that 𝒜m\mathcal{A}_{m} depends only on the Poisson processes associated to sites x≥y1x\geq y_{1} and on the Bernoulli variables associated to sites x>y1x>y_{1}. Hence we conclude that

ℙσΛ​({y1,…,yk}⊂𝒵⁡(σt)|ℱ)\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\bigl(\,\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})\thinspace|\thinspace\mathcal{F}\bigr) (4.3)
=ℙ(∪m=1∞(𝒜m∩{sy1,m=0})∩{{y2,…,yk}⊂𝒵(σt)|ℱ})\displaystyle={\mathbb{P}}\Big(\cup_{m=1}^{\infty}\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{m}\,\cap\{s_{y_{1},m}=0\}\bigr)\,\cap\bigl\{\{y_{2},\dots,y_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})\thinspace|\thinspace\mathcal{F}\bigr\}\Big)

OPEN⩽​q​ℙσΛ​({y2,…,yk}⊂𝒵⁡(σt))|ℱ).\displaystyle\;\leqslant\;q\,{\mathbb{P}}_{\sigma}^{\Lambda}\left(\{y_{2},\dots,y_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t}))\thinspace|\thinspace\mathcal{F}\right)\,.

A simple iteration clings the proof of (4.1).

Let us now consider the set Nt={t1,t2,…}N_{t}=\{t_{1},t_{2},\dots\} of all the occurrences up to time tt of the Poisson processes in VV and let |Nt||N_{t}| be its cardinality. Conditioned on NtN_{t} and ℱ\mathcal{F} the probability of seeing zeros located at {y1,y2,…,yk}\{y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{k}\} at a given time s∈Nts\in N_{t} is bounded from above by qkq^{k} because of exactly the same arguments that led to (4.1). Therefore

ℙσΛ(∃s≤t:{y1,…,yk}⊂𝒵(σs)|ℱ)⩽qk𝔼(|Nt||ℱ)=Ltqk.{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\bigl(\exists\,s\leq t:\ \bigl\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{s})\thinspace|\thinspace\mathcal{F}\bigr)\;\leqslant\;q^{k}{\mathbb{E}}(|N_{t}|\thinspace|\thinspace\mathcal{F})=Ltq^{k}\,.

because |Nt||N_{t}| is independent from ℱ\mathcal{F}. Thus (4.2) follows. The last statement in the lemma is trivial. ∎

Lemma 4.3 (Persistence of zeros).

Fix t>0t>0, σ∈ΩΛ\sigma\in\Omega_{\Lambda} and kk sites y1,…​yk∈Λy_{1},\dots y_{k}\in\Lambda. Then for any event 𝒜\mathcal{A} on D⁡([0,∞),ΩΛ)D([0,\infty),\Omega_{\Lambda})

The same result holds when Λ\Lambda is replaced by ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}.

Proof.

We can bound

ℙσΛ(𝒜∩{∀iyi∈𝒵(σt)})\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}(\mathcal{A}\cap\{\forall i\ y_{i}\in\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})\})

because of the strong Markov property and Lemma 4.2. Finally, we observe that the proof for the infinite volume East process is completely similar. ∎

Recall that σ0​𝟙∈ΩΛ\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}\in\Omega_{\Lambda} is the configuration with only one zero at the origin and that tn=1/qnt_{n}=1/q^{n} (see (2.4)).

Remark 4.2.

For L∈𝒞nL\in\mathcal{C}_{n} it follows from (4.8) that τ𝟙,τ~\tau_{\mathds{1}},\tilde{\tau} with high probability are smaller than tn1+δt_{n}^{1+\delta}, δ>0\delta>0. However, due to (4.7), we also have

limq↓0ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ𝟙<tn1−δ)=limq↓0ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ~<tn1−δ)=0.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}\left(\tau_{\mathds{1}}<t_{n}^{1-\delta}\right)=\lim_{q\downarrow 0}{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}\left(\tilde{\tau}<t_{n}^{1-\delta}\right)=0\,.

We state three useful consequences of the previous results. The first one (see Corollary 4.5 below) gives an upper bound on the probability of seeing a domain of class smaller or equal than nn at any fixed time independent of nn. The second and third one (see Corollary 4.6 and Corollary 4.7) upper bound the probability that one zero or at least two zeros disappear in a fixed time interval when the initial configuration has only zeros of class at most nn.

Corollary 4.5 (Domain survival probability).

Fix n​⩾​ 1n\;\geqslant\;1. Then there exists a positive constant c=c⁡(n,L)c=c(n,L) such that, for any σ∈ΩΛ\sigma\in\Omega_{\Lambda} and any x,y∈Λx,y\in\Lambda with x<yx<y and y−x​⩽​ 2ny-x\;\leqslant\;2^{n},

ℙσΛ({x,y}⊂𝒵(σt))⩽1min⁡(q,1−q)2nexp{−ct/tn}+2q,∀t⩾ 0.{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}(\{x,y\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t}))\;\leqslant\;\frac{1}{\min(q,1-q)^{2^{n}}}\exp\left\{-ct/t_{n}\right\}+2q\,,\qquad\forall t\;\geqslant\;0\,.

By using Lemma 4.3 we get

ℙσΛ​({x,y}⊂𝒵⁡(σt))​⩽​ 2​q+ℙσΛ​({x,y}⊂𝒵⁡(σs)​∀s∈[0,t]).{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}(\{x,y\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t}))\;\leqslant\;2q+{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}(\{x,y\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{s})~\forall s\in[0,t])\,.

Let σ¯:=σ[x,y−1]\bar{\sigma}:=\sigma_{[x,y-1]}. Then Lemma 2.2 and (iv) of Lemma 4.4 imply that

ℙσΛ​({x,y}⊂𝒵⁡(σs)​∀s∈[0,t])​⩽​ℙσ¯[x,y−1]​(τ~>t)\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\left(\{x,y\}\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{s})~\forall s\in[0,t]\right)\;\leqslant\;{\mathbb{P}}^{[x,y-1]}_{\bar{\sigma}}\left(\tilde{\tau}>t\right)
⩽1min⁡(q,1−q)y−xexp{−ct/tn}.∎\displaystyle\;\leqslant\;\frac{1}{\min(q,1-q)^{y-x}}\exp\left\{-ct/t_{n}\right\}\,.\qed
Corollary 4.6 (Killing at least one zero of class at least nn).

Fix n≥1n\geq 1. Consider the East process on Λ\Lambda starting from a configuration σ\sigma with a zero at x∈Λx\in\Lambda of class nx≥nn_{x}\geq n. Then there exists a positive constant c=c⁡(nx)c=c(n_{x}) such that

ℙσΛ​(x∉𝒵⁡(σt))​⩽​c​t/tn,∀t​⩾​ 0.{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\left(x\notin\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})\right)\;\leqslant\;ct/t_{n}\,,\qquad\forall t\;\geqslant\;0\,.

The same result holds with Λ\Lambda replaced by ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}.

Proof.

Let [x,y][x,y] be the domain in σ\sigma whose left boundary is xx. For simplicity of notation we restrict ourselves to the case y≤L−1y\leq L-1. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the Poisson processes and coin tosses associated to [y,L−1][y,L-1]. Then, thanks to Remark 4.1, in order to remove xx within time tt there must exists a time s≤ts\leq t such that |𝒵⁡(σs)∩(x,y)|≥n|\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{s})\cap(x,y)|\geq n. At this point the thesis follows from Lemma 4.2. The infinite volume case is similar. ∎

Corollary 4.7.

(Killing at least two zeros of class at least nn) Fix n​⩾​ 1n\;\geqslant\;1 and consider the East process on Λ\Lambda starting from a configuration σ\sigma with two zeros x<yx<y each of class nn. Define τn​(x)\tau_{n}(x) to be the first time such that in the interval (x,x+dx)(x,x+d_{x}) there are nn zeros. Similarly for yy. Then there exists a constant c=c⁡(n)c=c(n) such that

ℙσΛ​(τn​(x)≤t,τn​(y)≤t)≤c​(t/tn)2.{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}(\tau_{n}(x)\leq t\ ,\ \tau_{n}(y)\leq t)\leq c\left(t/t_{n}\right)^{2}. (4.10)

The same for the infinite volume case Λ→ℤ+\Lambda\to{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}. In particular, if the initial configuration σ\sigma has only zeros of class at least nn then

ℙσΛ({𝒵(σt)⊂𝒵(σ)}∩{|𝒵(σ)∖𝒵(σt)|⩾ 2})⩽c′(t/tn)2.\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\left(\{\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})\subset\mathcal{Z}(\sigma)\}\cap\{|\mathcal{Z}(\sigma)\setminus\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{t})|\;\geqslant\;2\}\right)\;\leqslant\;c^{\prime}\left(t/t_{n}\right)^{2}\,.

for some constant c′=c⁡(Λ,n)c^{\prime}=c(\Lambda,n).

Proof.

Call zz the next zero of σ\sigma immediately to the right of xx. Of course it is possible that z=yz=y and by assumption z=x+dxz=x+d_{x} with dx≥2n−1+1d_{x}\geq 2^{n-1}+1. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the σ\sigma-algebra of the Poisson processes and coin tosses associated to sites in [z,L−1][z,L-1]. Then

ℙσΛ(τn(x)≤t,τn(y)≤t)=𝔼(1I{τn(y)≤t}ℙσΛ(τn(x)≤t|ℱ))≤c(t/tn)2{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}(\tau_{n}(x)\leq t\ ,\ \tau_{n}(y)\leq t)={\mathbb{E}}\left({1\mskip-5.0mu{\rm I}}_{\{\tau_{n}(y)\leq t\}}{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}(\tau_{n}(x)\leq t\thinspace|\thinspace\mathcal{F})\right)\leq c(t/t_{n})^{2}

because of (4.7). Similarly when Λ\Lambda is replaced by ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}. The second conclusion is now immediate once we appeal to Remark 4.1. Indeed, in order to remove within time tt two zeros x,yx,y of class at least nn, their respective stopping times τn​(x),τn​(y)\tau_{n}(x),\tau_{n}(y) must have occurred before time tt.

∎

Before moving on we summarize the overall picture that emerges from the above results into a single proposition.

Proposition 4.8.

Consider the East process on Λ\Lambda starting from a configuration σ\sigma. Fix a large integer NN, fix ϵ​⩽​(8​N)−1\epsilon\;\leqslant\;(8N)^{-1} and let tn±:=(1/q)n⁡(1±ϵ)t_{n}^{\pm}:=(1/q)^{n(1\pm\epsilon)}. Notice that tn−≫tn−1+t_{n}^{-}\gg t_{n-1}^{+} for n​⩽​Nn\;\leqslant\;N and small qq. Then the following picture up to scale NN holds with probability tending to one as q↓0q\downarrow 0.

  • •

    The typical time necessary to kill a zero of class nn is of order tn1+o⁡(1)t_{n}^{1+o(1)} so that at time tn−t_{n}^{-} the zeros of σ\sigma of class at least nn are still present.

  • •

    At time t​⩾​tn+t\;\geqslant\;t_{n}^{+} all zeros are of class at least n+1n+1 (and thus at time t​⩾​tn−t\;\geqslant\;t^{-}_{n} of class at least nn).

  • •

    Split the active period [tn−,tn+][t_{n}^{-},t_{n}^{+}] into disjoint sub-periods of width TnT_{n} defined in (3.3). Then in each sub-period at most one zero of class nn is killed.

The last property follows by a simple application of Corollary 4.7.

4.1.1. Proof of Lemma 4.4

We are now left with the proof of Lemma 4.4 and for this purpose we need first two preliminary results. Recall that πΛ\pi_{\Lambda} denotes the product Bernoulli measure on ΩΛ\Omega_{\Lambda} with density 1−q1-q.

Lemma 4.9.

For any A⊂ΩΛA\subset\Omega_{\Lambda}, the hitting time τA=inf{t​⩾​ 0:σt∈A}\tau_{A}=\inf\{t\;\geqslant\;0:\sigma_{t}\in A\} satisfies

ℙπΛΛ(τA>t)⩽e−tgap(ℒΛ)πΛ(A).{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\pi_{\Lambda}}(\tau_{A}>t)\;\leqslant\;e^{-t\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}_{\Lambda})\pi_{\Lambda}(A)}\,.
Proof.

It is well known (see e.g. [2]) that ℙπΛL​(τA>t)​⩽​e−t​λA{\mathbb{P}}^{L}_{\pi_{\Lambda}}(\tau_{A}>t)\;\leqslant\;e^{-t\lambda_{A}}, where

λA:=inf{𝒟Λ​(f):πΛ​(f2)=1​ and ​f≡0​ on ​A},\lambda_{A}:=\inf\left\{\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}(f):\pi_{\Lambda}(f^{2})=1\mbox{ and }f\equiv 0\mbox{ on }A\right\}\,,

𝒟Λ​(f)=−πΛ​(f,ℒΛ​f)\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}(f)=-\pi_{\Lambda}(f,\mathcal{L}_{\Lambda}f) being the Dirichlet form of ff. Since VarΛ(f)/πΛ​(f2)≥πΛ​(A)\mathop{\rm Var}\nolimits_{\Lambda}(f)/\pi_{\Lambda}(f^{2})\geq\pi_{\Lambda}(A) if f≡0f\equiv 0 on AA, from the definition of the spectral gap

gap(ℒΛ):=inff:πΛ​(f)=0𝒟Λ​(f)πΛ​(f2),\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}_{\Lambda}):=\inf_{f:\ \pi_{\Lambda}(f)=0}\;\frac{\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}(f)}{\pi_{\Lambda}(f^{2})}\,, (4.11)

it follows immediately that λA​⩾​gap(ℒΛ)​πΛ​(A)\lambda_{A}\;\geqslant\;\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}_{\Lambda})\pi_{\Lambda}(A). ∎

In order to use the former result we will need in turn a sharp lower bound on the spectral gap on finite volume.

Lemma 4.10.

Recall that Λ=[0,L−1]\Lambda=[0,L-1]. Then, for any integers n,Ln,L with 1​⩽​L​⩽​ 2n1\;\leqslant\;L\;\leqslant\;2^{n},

gap(ℒΛ)​⩾​(q2)n.\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}_{\Lambda})\;\geqslant\;\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^{n}.
Proof.

Fix n,Ln,L as above. We first observe that, by monotonicity of the gap for the East model (see [4, Lemma 2.11]) it is enough to consider the case L=2nL=2^{n}. For lightness of notation we denote by γn\gamma_{n} the inverse gap on [0,2n−1][0,2^{n}-1] (with a frozen zero at L=2nL=2^{n}). The result is obtained by induction, following the bisection constrained method introduced in [4].

Let A=[0,2n−1−1]A=[0,2^{n-1}-1] and B=[2n−1,2n−1]B=[2^{n-1},2^{n}-1] and set a=2n−1a=2^{n-1}. Notice that Λ:=[0,2n−1]=A∪B\Lambda:=[0,2^{n}-1]=A\cup B, A∩B=∅A\cap B=\emptyset and that gap(ℒA)−1=gap(ℒB)−1=γn−1\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}_{A})^{-1}=\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits(\mathcal{L}_{B})^{-1}=\gamma_{n-1}. We will denote by VarΛ⁡(f)\operatorname{Var}_{\Lambda}(f), πΛ​(f)\pi_{\Lambda}(f) and 𝒟Λ​(f)\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}(f) the variance, mean and Dirichlet form of ff on the interval Λ\Lambda. Analogous notation hold for the same quantities restricted to the intervals AA and BB.

Consider the following auxiliary ”constrained block dynamics”. The block BB waits a mean one exponential random time and then the current configuration inside it is refreshed with a new one sampled from πB\pi_{B}. The block AA does the same but now the configuration is refreshed only if the current configuration σ\sigma is such that σ⁡(a)=0\sigma(a)=0. The Dirichlet form of this new chain is

𝒟block​(f)=πΛ​(cA​VarA⁡(f)+VarB⁡(f))\mathcal{D}_{\rm block}(f)=\pi_{\Lambda}\left(c_{A}\operatorname{Var}_{A}(f)+\operatorname{Var}_{B}(f)\right)

with cA​(σ)=1−σ⁡(a)c_{A}(\sigma)=1-\sigma(a). If gapblock\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm block} is the corresponding spectral gap then Proposition 4.4 in [4] gives

gapblock⩾​ 1−1−q​⩾​q2.\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm block}\;\geqslant\;1-\sqrt{1-q}\;\geqslant\;\frac{q}{2}\,.

Hence,

VarΛ⁡(f)​⩽​2q​πΛ​(cA​VarA⁡(f)+VarB⁡(f)).\operatorname{Var}_{\Lambda}(f)\;\leqslant\;\frac{2}{q}\pi_{\Lambda}\left(c_{A}\operatorname{Var}_{A}(f)+\operatorname{Var}_{B}(f)\right).

Now VarB⁡(f)​⩽​γn−1​𝒟B​(f)\operatorname{Var}_{B}(f)\;\leqslant\;\gamma_{n-1}\mathcal{D}_{B}(f) and, by construction, (see (2.2)) cxB=cxΛc_{x}^{B}=c_{x}^{\Lambda} for any x∈Bx\in B. Therefore

πΛ​(VarB⁡(f))​⩽​γn−1​∑x∈BcxΛ​Varx⁡(f)\pi_{\Lambda}\left(\operatorname{Var}_{B}(f)\right)\;\leqslant\;\gamma_{n-1}\sum_{x\in B}c_{x}^{\Lambda}\operatorname{Var}_{x}(f)

which is nothing but the contribution carried by BB to the full Dirichlet form 𝒟Λ​(f)\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}(f). As far as the block AA is concerned one observes that cxA⋅cA=cxΛc_{x}^{A}\cdot c_{A}=c_{x}^{\Lambda} for any x∈Ax\in A. In conclusion

VarΛ⁡(f)​⩽​2q​γn−1​𝒟Λ​(f)i.e. γn​⩽​2q​γn−1.\operatorname{Var}_{\Lambda}(f)\;\leqslant\;\frac{2}{q}\gamma_{n-1}\mathcal{D}_{\Lambda}(f)\quad\text{\hbox{\it i.e.\ }}\quad\gamma_{n}\;\leqslant\;\frac{2}{q}\ \gamma_{n-1}.

Since γ0=1\gamma_{0}=1 the result follows immediately. ∎

Remark 4.3.

The above result leads to the lower bound g​a​p​(ℒΛ)=(q2)log2⁡(1/q)gap(\mathcal{L}_{\Lambda})=\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)^{\log_{2}(1/q)} when nn is of the order log⁡2/log⁡(1/q)\log 2/\log(1/q), namely when the length of Λ\Lambda becomes of the order of the equilibrium domains. We stress that this is not the correct scaling on this length, which is instead (q)log2⁡(1/q)/2\left(q\right)^{\log_{2}(1/q)/2} as proven in Section 6 of [4] for the lower bound and in Appendix 5 of [5] for the upper bound. Indeed, the above described bisection-technique should be refined as described in [4] to capture the correct scaling up to this length. However, for the purpose of this paper the above easier bound is enough (and this because we do analyze here the evolution at times much smaller than the global relaxation time).

Proof of Lemma 4.4.

(i) The proof is straightforward. (ii) Trivially τ𝟙​⩽​τ~\tau_{\mathds{1}}\;\leqslant\;\tilde{\tau}. On the other hand, if the starting configuration is σ0​𝟙\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}, Remark 4.1 implies at once that τn​⩽​τ~\tau_{n}\;\leqslant\;\tilde{\tau}. (iii) Thanks to (ii) we have

ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ𝟙<t)​⩽​ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ~<t)​⩽​ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τn<t).\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\tau_{\mathds{1}}<t)\;\leqslant\;{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\tilde{\tau}<t)\;\leqslant\;{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\tau_{n}<t)\,.

The last probability is bounded from above by c​t/tnct/t_{n} with c=(L−1n)c=\binom{L-1}{n} by (4.2) in Lemma 4.2. (iv) Trivially (4.9) follows from (4.8). The proof of (4.8) is based on Lemma 4.9 with A={σ𝟙}A=\{\sigma_{\mathds{1}}\}, and on Lemma 4.10. We get

ℙσΛ​(τ𝟙>t)​⩽​1πΛ​(σ)​ℙπΛΛ​(τ𝟙>t)\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}(\tau_{\mathds{1}}>t)\;\leqslant\;\frac{1}{\pi_{\Lambda}(\sigma)}{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\pi_{\Lambda}}(\tau_{\mathds{1}}>t)

with c:=(1/2)2n/2nc:=(1/2)^{2^{n}}/2^{n}. ∎

4.1.2. Approximate exponentiality of the hitting time τ~\tilde{\tau}

As it is very often the case for systems showing metastable behavior (see e.g. [24]), a loss of memory mechanism produces activation times that become exponential variables after appropriate rescaling. In our case the appropriate activation time is the hitting time τ~:=inf{t​⩾​ 0:σt​(0)=1}\tilde{\tau}:=\inf\{t\;\geqslant\;0:\sigma_{t}(0)=1\}.

Lemma 4.11.

Let f⁡(t):=ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ~/γ>t),f(t):={\mathbb{P}}_{0\mathds{1}}^{\Lambda}\left(\tilde{\tau}/\gamma>t\right)\,, where γ=γ⁡(q,Λ)\gamma=\gamma(q,\Lambda) is such that f⁡(1)=e−1f(1)=e^{-1}. Then, for any t,s​⩾​ 0t,s\;\geqslant\;0, it holds

|f⁡(t+s)−f⁡(s)​f​(t)|≤c​q|f(t+s)-f(s)f(t)|\leq cq (4.12)

for some constant c>0c>0 independent of qq. In particular, for any t>0t>0, limq↓0f⁡(t)=e−t\lim_{q\downarrow 0}f(t)=e^{-t}.

Proof.

That limq↓0f⁡(t)=e−t\lim_{q\downarrow 0}f(t)=e^{-t} follows from (4.12) by standard arguments (see e.g. [25]). We now prove (4.12). For any s,t​⩾​ 0s,t\;\geqslant\;0 we have

f⁡(t+s)=ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ~>γ⁡(t+s)|τ~>γ​s)​f​(s).f(t+s)={\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\tilde{\tau}>\gamma(t+s)\thinspace|\thinspace\tilde{\tau}>\gamma s)f(s).

Moreover, thanks to the Markov property,

ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ~>γ⁡(t+s)|τ~>γ​s)=f⁡(t)​ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(σs​γ=σ0​𝟙|τ~>γ​s)+ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(τ~>γ⁡(t+s)|τ~>γ​s;σγ​s≠σ0​𝟙)​ℙ0​𝟙Λ​(σγ​s≠σ0​𝟙|τ~>γ​s),{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\tilde{\tau}>\gamma(t+s)\thinspace|\thinspace\tilde{\tau}>\gamma s)=f(t)\,{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\sigma_{s\gamma}=\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}\thinspace|\thinspace\tilde{\tau}>\gamma s)\\ +{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\tilde{\tau}>\gamma(t+s)\thinspace|\thinspace\tilde{\tau}>\gamma s\,;\,\sigma_{\gamma s}\neq\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}){\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\sigma_{\gamma s}\neq\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}|\tilde{\tau}>\gamma s)\,, (4.13)

and therefore

|f(t+s)−f(t)f(s)|≤2ℙ0​𝟙Λ({σs​γ≠σ0​𝟙}∩{τ~>γs})≤2Lq.\displaystyle|f(t+s)-f(t)f(s)|\leq 2{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{0\mathds{1}}(\{\sigma_{s\gamma}\neq\sigma_{0\mathds{1}}\}\cap\{\tilde{\tau}>\gamma s\})\leq 2Lq\,.

where we used Lemma 4.2 in the last inequality. ∎

Remark 4.4.

If Λ=[0,L−1]\Lambda=[0,L-1] with L∈𝒞nL\in\mathcal{C}_{n}\,, then by using Remark 4.2 we obtain γ=tn1+o⁡(1)\gamma=t_{n}^{1+o(1)} as q↓0q\downarrow 0.

4.2. Finite volume approximation

In this section we prove a finite volume approximation result of the infinite volume East process with initial distribution Q=Ren​(ν,μ)Q=\text{Ren}(\nu,\mu), provided that μ⁡([n,∞))>0\mu\left([n,\infty)\right)>0 for any nn.

Proposition 4.12.

Let Q=Ren​(ν,μ)Q=\text{Ren}(\nu,\mu) and suppose that μ⁡([n,∞))>0\mu\left([n,\infty)\right)>0 for any nn. Then, for any ℓ\ell and any NN,

limL↑∞lim supq↓0supt∈[0,tN+]d⁡(t,ℓ,L)=0\lim_{L\uparrow\infty}\limsup_{q\downarrow 0}\sup_{t\in[0,t^{+}_{N}]}d(t,\ell,L)=0

where d⁡(t,ℓ,L)d(t,\ell,L) denotes the variation distance between the laws of the vector (σ⁡(0),…,σ⁡(ℓ))\left(\sigma(0),\dots,\sigma(\ell)\right) at time tt for the East process in Λ=[0,L−1]\Lambda=[0,L-1] and the East process in ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} with initial distribution QQ.

Proof.

Let n0≥N+1n_{0}\geq N+1 be such that μ⁡(2n0)>0\mu(2^{n_{0}})>0 and let

𝒜L:={σ∈Ω:∃xj∈𝒵(σ)∩[ℓ+1,L−2n0] of class n0}.\mathcal{A}_{L}:=\{\sigma\in\Omega:\ \exists\,x_{j}\in\mathcal{Z}(\sigma)\cap[\ell+1,L-2^{n_{0}}]\text{ of class $n_{0}$}\}\,.

From the renewal property of QQ it follows that limL→∞Q⁡(𝒜L)=1\lim_{L\to\infty}Q\left(\mathcal{A}_{L}\right)=1. For any σ∈𝒜L\sigma\in\mathcal{A}_{L} let x∗∈[ℓ+1,L−2n0]x_{*}\in[\ell+1,L-2^{n_{0}}] be the smallest zero of σ\sigma of class n0n_{0}. Since n0≥N+1n_{0}\geq N+1 Corollary 4.6 (see also Proposition 4.8) implies that x∗∈𝒵⁡(σs)​∀s≤tNx_{*}\in\mathcal{Z}(\sigma_{s})\ \forall s\leq t_{N} with probability tending to one as q↓0q\downarrow 0 both for the finite and infinite volume East processes starting from σ\sigma. Finally, conditioned to the event that for both processes x∗x_{*} is not killed up to time tNt_{N}, the graphical construction implies that their evolutions in [0,ℓ][0,\ell] coincide up to time tNt_{N}. ∎

In order to state the next result it is convenient to define, for any Λ=[0,L−1]\Lambda=[0,L-1], xkΛ:=xk​(σ)x_{k}^{\Lambda}:=x_{k}(\sigma) if |𝒵⁡(σ)∩Λ|≥k|\mathcal{Z}(\sigma)\cap\Lambda|\geq k and xkΛ=Lx_{k}^{\Lambda}=L otherwise.

Proposition 4.13.

Let Q=Ren​(ν,μ)Q=\text{Ren}(\nu,\mu) and suppose that μ⁡([n,∞))>0\mu\left([n,\infty)\right)>0 for any nn. Then for any N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} and k≥0k\geq 0 it holds: (i)

limL↑∞lim supq↓0supt∈[0,tN+]dT​V​({(x0​(t),…,xk​(t)),ℙQ},{(x0Λ​(t),…,xkΛ​(t)),ℙQΛ})=0.\lim_{L\uparrow\infty}\limsup_{q\downarrow 0}\,\sup_{t\in[0,t^{+}_{N}]}\,d_{TV}\bigl(\,\{(x_{0}(t),\dots,x_{k}(t)),\,{\mathbb{P}}_{Q}\}\,;\,\{(x^{\Lambda}_{0}(t),\dots,x^{\Lambda}_{k}(t)),\,{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{Q}\}\bigr)=0\,. (4.14)

(ii) If the (m+δ)t​h(m+\delta)^{th}-moments of ν,μ\nu,\mu are both finite for some δ>0\delta>0 then

and

Proof.

Let us fix NN and n0≥N+1n_{0}\geq N+1 such that μ0:=μ⁡(2n0)>0\mu_{0}:=\mu(2^{n_{0}})>0. (i) Fix kk and L≫k​2n0L\gg k2^{n_{0}}, and consider the event

Clearly limL↑∞Q⁡(ℬk,L)=1\lim_{L\uparrow\infty}Q\left(\mathcal{B}_{k,L}\right)=1. For σ∈ℬk,L\sigma\in\mathcal{B}_{k,L} let {x∗(i)}i=0k\{x_{*}^{(i)}\}_{i=0}^{k} be the smallest zeros with the properties described in ℬk,L\mathcal{B}_{k,L}. Since the conditioning event has probability tending to one as q↓0q\downarrow 0 thanks to Corollary 4.6 (both for the East process on Λ\Lambda and the infinite volume East process) the thesis follows.

(ii)-(4.15) For simplicity and without loss of generality we only discuss the case k=0k=0. The argument here is conceptually similar to that employed in the proof of (i) but more involved. The reason is that, in order to have a good control on the probability ℙQ​(x1​(t)−x0​(t)≥ℓ){\mathbb{P}}_{Q}(x_{1}(t)-x_{0}(t)\geq\ell), ℓ\ell very large even compared to e.g. 1/q1/q, a single zero at time t=0t=0 of class at least n0n_{0} is no longer enough. Remark 4.5.

The same results of Propositions 4.12 and 4.13 hold for the hierarchical coalescence process HCP and the proof is practically the same with one big simplification. As soon as a zero of class bigger than NN occurs in the initial configuration, then, up to time tNt_{N}, the zero cannot be erased. Thus, in this case, the uniform bound on, say, 𝔼Q​(x1​(t)m){\mathbb{E}}_{Q}(x_{1}(t)^{m}) are all obtained through a control of the corresponding mt​hm^{th}-moment of QQ without any need of “dynamical” estimates.

5. East process and HCP: proof of Theorems 3.7 and 3.8

As already mentioned at the end of Section 3.5, the proof of Theorem 3.8 follows at once from Theorem 3.7 together with Propositions 4.12 and 4.13 and their analog for the HCP process (see Remark 4.5). Thus the key point here is to prove Theorem 3.7.

Without loss of generality we can assume that (the label of) the largest epoch NN which we will observe is larger than one and that ϵ=1/8​N\epsilon=1/8N. We will show below that the proof of the theorem can be reduced to the proof of the following claim.

Claim 5.1.

Let σ∈ΩΛ\sigma\in\Omega_{\Lambda} be such that any zero in 𝒵⁡(σ)\mathcal{Z}(\sigma) is of class at least nn. Then

limq↓0supt∈[0,tn+−tn−]dT​V​({σt,ℙσΛ},{σt,ℙσΛ,n,C})=0\lim_{q\downarrow 0}\sup_{t\in[0,t_{n}^{+}-t_{n}^{-}]}d_{TV}\left(\{\sigma_{t},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\}\,;\,\{\sigma_{t},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda,n,C}_{\sigma}\}\right)=0

where we recall ℙσΛ,n,C{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda,n,C}_{\sigma} denotes the law of the nt​hn^{th}-coalescence process on Λ\Lambda starting from σ\sigma and defined in Section 3.2 with the choice ϵ=1/8​N\epsilon=1/8N.

Let us explain how to derive Theorem 3.7 assuming the claim. Fixed t≤tN+t\leq t_{N}^{+}, there are two cases to be examined:

  1. (a)

    tt belongs to an active period i.e. t∈[tn−,tn+]t\in[t_{n}^{-},t_{n}^{+}];

  2. (b)

    tt belongs to a stalling period i.e. t∈[tn−1+,tn−]t\in[t_{n-1}^{+},t_{n}^{-}].

We first observe that during a stalling period nothing happens with probability tending to one as q↓0q\downarrow 0. More precisely, for any σ∈ΩΛ\sigma\in\Omega_{\Lambda}, by using Proposition 4.8 we get

limq↓0supn≤Nsupt∈[tn−1+,tn−]dT​V​({σt,ℙσΛ},{σtn−1+,ℙσΛ})=0\lim_{q\downarrow 0}\sup_{n\leq N}\sup_{t\in[t_{n-1}^{+},t_{n}^{-}]}d_{TV}\left(\{\sigma_{t},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\}\,;\,\{\sigma_{t_{n-1}^{+}},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\}\right)=0 (5.1)

and similarly for the HCP process by using Corollary 3.5.

Thus, by a simple triangular inequality for the variation distance, it is enough to consider only case (a). For this purpose we first observe that, thanks to the Markov property, to the fact that with probability tending to one as q↓0q\downarrow 0 all the zeros of σtn−\sigma_{t_{n}^{-}} are of class at least nn (Corollary 3.5 and Proposition 4.8) and to Claim 5.1,

limq↓0sups∈[0,tn+−tn−]dT​V​({σtn−+s,ℙσΛ},{σtn−+s,ℙσΛ,H})=0\lim_{q\downarrow 0}\sup_{s\in[0,t_{n}^{+}-t_{n}^{-}]}d_{TV}\left(\{\sigma_{t^{-}_{n}+s},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\}\,;\,\{\sigma_{t^{-}_{n}+s},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda,H}_{\sigma}\}\right)=0

if

limq↓0dT​V​({σtn−,ℙσΛ},{σtn−,ℙσΛ,H})=0.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}d_{TV}\left(\{\sigma_{t^{-}_{n}},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\}\,;\,\{\sigma_{t^{-}_{n}},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda,H}_{\sigma}\}\right)=0\,.

In turn, thanks to (5.1), the above holds if

limq↓0dT​V​({σtn−1+,ℙσΛ},{σtn−1+,ℙσΛ,H})=0.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}d_{TV}\left(\{\sigma_{t^{+}_{n-1}},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda}_{\sigma}\}\,;\,\{\sigma_{t^{+}_{n-1}},{\mathbb{P}}^{\Lambda,H}_{\sigma}\}\right)=0\,. (5.2)

If we recursively iterate the above argument (note that when n−1=0n-1=0 (5.2) holds from Claim 5.1 since t0−=0t_{0}^{-}=0) we get the sought conclusion. Thus the proofs of Theorem 3.7 and 3.8 are completed once we prove Claim 5.1.

7. Extensions

In this section we present some extensions of our results. As already mentioned, the technical assumption that the interval law μ\mu satisfies μ⁡([k,∞))>0\mu([k,\infty))>0 for all k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} can be removed as discussed in [15]. As a consequence, in what follows we disregard this assumption.

7.1. The East process on ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} with renewal stationary initial distribution

We say that a random subset σ\sigma of ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} is stationary if its law QQ is left invariant by any translation along a vector x∈ℤx\in{\mathbb{Z}}. In addition, we say that it is renewal if the law Q(⋅| 0∈σ)Q(\cdot\thinspace|\thinspace 0\in\sigma) equals Ren⁡(μ| 0){\rm Ren}(\mu\thinspace|\thinspace 0) for some probability measure on ℕ{\mathbb{N}} (note that Q⁡(0∈σ)Q(0\in\sigma) must be positive due to the stationarity). For simplicity, we write Q=Ren⁡(μ)Q={\rm Ren}(\mu) and call μ\mu the interval law. Note that under the Bernoulli probability on {0,1}ℤ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{Z}} with parameter pp, the set of zeros has law Ren⁡(μ| 0){\rm Ren}(\mu\thinspace|\thinspace 0) with μ⁡(n)=pn−1​(1−p)\mu(n)=p^{n-1}(1-p).

It can be proved (see [9]) that μ\mu must have finite mean. Moreover, QQ–a.s. the random subset σ\sigma is given by infinite points {xk}k∈ℤ\{x_{k}\}_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}} with limk→±∞xk=±∞\lim_{k\to\pm\infty}x_{k}=\pm\infty. In what follows, we enumerate the points in σ\sigma with the convention that xk<xk+1x_{k}<x_{k+1} and x0​⩽​ 0<x1x_{0}\;\leqslant\;0<x_{1}.

Due to formula (C3) in [14, Appendix C] the set σ\sigma with law Q=Ren⁡(μ)Q={\rm Ren}(\mu) is characterized by the following properties:

  • (i)

    the points x0​⩽​ 0<x1x_{0}\;\leqslant\;0<x_{1} have law

    Q⁡(x0​⩽−m,x1​⩾​n)=(1/μ¯)​∑ℓ=n+m∞μ⁡(ℓ)​(ℓ−n−m+1)=(1/μ¯)​∑ℓ=n+m∞μ⁡([ℓ,∞))\begin{split}Q(x_{0}\;\leqslant\;-m\,,\;x_{1}\;\geqslant\;n)&=(1/\bar{\mu})\sum_{\ell=n+m}^{\infty}\mu(\ell)(\ell-n-m+1)\\ &=(1/\bar{\mu})\sum_{\ell=n+m}^{\infty}\mu([\ell,\infty))\end{split} (7.1)

    for all n​⩾​ 1,m​⩾​ 0n\;\geqslant\;1,m\;\geqslant\;0, where μ¯\bar{\mu} denotes the average of μ\mu: μ¯=∑ℓ=1∞μ⁡(ℓ)​ℓ\bar{\mu}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}\mu(\ell)\ell;

  • (ii)

    the domain lengths (xk+1−xk)(x_{k+1}-x_{k}), k∈ℤ∖{0}k\in{\mathbb{Z}}\setminus\{0\}, are i.i.d. random variables with law μ\mu and are also independent from x0,x1x_{0},x_{1}.

Note that (7.1) implies that Q⁡(0∈ξ)=1/μ¯Q(0\in\xi)=1/\bar{\mu} and that |x0|+1|x_{0}|+1 has the same law of x1x_{1}. Due to the above characterization, under Q=Ren⁡(μ)Q={\rm Ren}(\mu) the law of σ∩ℤ+\sigma\cap{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} is given by Q+=Ren⁡(ν,μ)Q_{+}={\rm Ren}(\nu,\mu), where ν\nu is the probability measure on ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} such that

ν(n)=(1/μ¯)μ([n+1,∞)),n∈ℤ+\nu(n)=(1/\bar{\mu})\mu([n+1,\infty))\,,\qquad n\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}

(indeed by stationarity ν\nu coincides with the law of x1−1x_{1}-1 since x1x_{1} is the leftmost point of σ∩ℕ\sigma\cap{\mathbb{N}}). Note that ν\nu has finite mt​hm^{th}–moment if and only if μ\mu has finite (m+1)t​h(m+1)^{th}-moment.

The above observation implies that Theorem 2.5 can be adapted to the stationary case following the guidelines of Remark 2.3.

The East process starting from QQ must be compared with the hierarchical coalescence process on ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} starting from QQ (the definition is a straightforward extension of the one given for the HCP on ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}). In [14] it is proved that, considering the HCP on ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} starting with distribution Q=Ren⁡(μ)Q={\rm Ren}(\mu), the law at the beginning of the nn–th epoch is simply Ren⁡(μn){\rm Ren}(\mu_{n}) with μn\mu_{n} defined from μ\mu as in Subsection 3.4.

By slightly modifications in the proof, Theorem 3.8 becomes:

Theorem 7.1.

For any N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} let ϵN:=1/8​N\epsilon_{N}:=1/8N and choose the parameter ϵ\epsilon appearing in Definition 2.4 and in (3.3) equal to ϵN\epsilon_{N}. Let Q=Ren​(μ)Q=\text{Ren}(\mu) with μ\mu probability measure on ℕ{\mathbb{N}} having finite mean. Then for any k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}}

limq↓0supt∈[0,tN+]dT​V​({(x−k​(t),…,xk​(t)),ℙQ},{(x−kH​(t),…,xkH​(t)),ℙQH})=0.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}\,\sup_{t\in[0,t_{N}^{+}]}\,d_{TV}\bigl(\,\{(x_{-k}(t),\dots,x_{k}(t)),\,{\mathbb{P}}_{Q}\}\,;\,\{(x^{H}_{-k}(t),\dots,x^{H}_{k}(t)),\,{\mathbb{P}}^{H}_{Q}\}\bigr)=0\,.

Assume that the (m+δ)t​h(m+\delta)^{th}-moment of μ\mu is finite for some δ>0\delta>0. Then, for each k∈ℤ∖{0}k\in{\mathbb{Z}}\setminus\{0\} it holds

limq↓0supt∈[0,tN+]|𝔼Q​([xk+1​(t)−xk​(t)]m)−𝔼QH​([xk+1H​(t)−xkH​(t)]m)|=0.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}\sup_{t\in[0,t_{N}^{+}]}\bigl|{\mathbb{E}}_{Q}\bigl([x_{k+1}(t)-x_{k}(t)]^{m}\bigr)-{\mathbb{E}}_{Q}^{\text{H}}\bigl([x^{H}_{k+1}(t)-x^{H}_{k}(t)]^{m}\bigr)\bigr|=0\,.

Assume that the (m+1+δ)t​h(m+1+\delta)^{th}-moment of μ\mu is finite for some δ>0\delta>0. Then the above equation (3.26) is valid also for k=0k=0 and moreover, for all k∈ℤk\in{\mathbb{Z}}, it holds

limq↓0supt∈[0,tN+]|𝔼Q​([xk​(t)]m)−𝔼QH​([xkH​(t)]m)|=0.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}\sup_{t\in[0,t_{N}^{+}]}\bigl|{\mathbb{E}}_{Q}\bigl([x_{k}(t)]^{m}\bigr)-{\mathbb{E}}_{Q}^{\text{H}}\bigl([x^{H}_{k}(t)]^{m}\bigr)\bigr|=0\,.

Using the above approximation result and the scaling limits discussed in [14], Theorem 2.6 remains valid in the stationary case by setting

X¯(n)​(t):=(xk+1​(t)−xk​(t))/(2n−1+1);Y¯(n)​(t):=x1​(t)/(2n−1+1),\bar{X}^{(n)}(t):=(x_{k+1}(t)-x_{k}(t))/(2^{n-1}+1)\quad;\quad\bar{Y}^{(n)}(t):=x_{1}(t)/(2^{n-1}+1),

where kk is any integer in ℤ∖{0}{\mathbb{Z}}\setminus\{0\}. Y¯(n)​(t)\bar{Y}^{(n)}(t) can also be defined as |x0​(t)|/(2n−1+1)|x_{0}(t)|/(2^{n-1}+1).

Remark 7.1.

The above extensions to the stationary case, and their derivation, will be discussed in more detail in [15]. There we will present other results, including the aging through hierarchical coalescence in the East process on the half–line {−1,−2,…}\{-1,-2,\dots\} with frozen zero at site 00.

7.2. The East process on ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} with exchangeable initial distribution

Our main results, with suitable modifications, can be formulated also when the initial distribution in an exchangeable one. We say that the law QQ of a random set of points {xi}i=0∞\{x_{i}\}_{i=0}^{\infty} in ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} containing the origin is exchangeable if this set has infinite cardinality a.s. and the law of the random sequence x1−x0=x1x_{1}-x_{0}=x_{1}, x2−x1x_{2}-x_{1}, x3−x2x_{3}-x_{2},… is invariant w.r.t. finite permutations. By De Finetti Theorem, QQ can be expressed as Q=∫Υ𝔭⁡(𝑑ζ)​QζQ=\int_{\Upsilon}\mathfrak{p}(d\zeta)Q_{\zeta}, where Qζ=Ren⁡(μζ| 0)Q_{\zeta}={\rm Ren}(\mu_{\zeta}\thinspace|\thinspace 0) and the parameter ζ\zeta varies on a probability space (Υ,𝔭)(\Upsilon,\mathfrak{p}) [14, Appendix D].

Considering the East process on ℤ+{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} with initial distribution QQ, suppose that for 𝔭\mathfrak{p}–a.a. ζ∈Υ\zeta\in\Upsilon the law μζ\mu_{\zeta} satisfies condition (a) or (b) in Theorem 2.5, set c0​(ζ)=1c_{0}(\zeta)=1 and c0​(ζ)=αc_{0}(\zeta)=\alpha respectively. Then Theorem 2.5 remains valid introducing in the asymptotic values the average ∫Υ𝔭⁡(𝑑ζ)\int_{\Upsilon}\mathfrak{p}(d\zeta) and replacing c0c_{0} with c0​(ζ)c_{0}(\zeta) and ρx\rho_{x} with Qζ​(σ​(x)=0)Q_{\zeta}(\sigma(x)=0). By similar modifications, also Theorem 2.6 remains valid for an exchangeable QQ. Clearly, the average over 𝔭⁡(d​ζ)\mathfrak{p}(d\zeta) may lead to new asymptotic behaviors. Finally, Theorem 3.8 still holds provided that the (m+δ)t​h(m+\delta)^{th}-moment w.r.t QQ of (xk+1−xk)(x_{k+1}-x_{k}) (which is kk–independent by exchangeability) is finite.
